definition: Renunciation means the formal, deliberate giving up of a right, claim, title, or belief.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word renunciation. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know renunciation should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Signing the oath at the consulate, Priya completed her renunciation of her old citizenship, knowing the decision was permanent.
A waiver is weaker — it gives up one specific right, often as routine paperwork, without renunciation's sense of a solemn, life-changing break.
Abdication is stronger — it is the renunciation of the highest office itself, surrendering not just a single claim but supreme power.

A disavowal formally denies any connection to or responsibility for something — a campaign disavows a supporter's remarks: 'that is not ours.' Renunciation gives up something that genuinely is yours — a right, title, or belief you admit you hold and now formally release. Disavowal says it was never mine; renunciation says it is mine no longer.

Surrender is the act of handing over or giving up something you held, often because pressure or defeat leaves little choice. Renunciation is deliberate and declared: a formal, often written act of giving up a right, claim, or belief of your own free will. Armies surrender; monks and ex-monarchs make renunciations.

Abandonment is giving something up completely and leaving it behind — walking away from a car, a plan, a post — with no ceremony and no formal declaration. Renunciation is the opposite in style: a solemn, declared, often signed act of giving up a right, claim, or belief.

Renunciation fits because Marcus is formally and deliberately giving up a legal claim — a share of future profits — and the act is made official in a signed document, not just a casual decision to walk away.
Formal / legal & religious
Renunciation is a formal, official word — it appears in citizenship law, legal filings, and religious life, and it implies a deliberate, declared act.
You make a renunciation of a claim, title, belief, or allegiance; giving up snacks for a week is just quitting, not a renunciation.

When her grandfather's estate passed to her at twenty-nine, Maren Voss surprised everyone by beginning the paperwork of renunciation the very same month.
The inheritance was legally hers, and no court, creditor, or relative was pressing her to give it up.
Yet she appeared before a notary, read a two-page declaration aloud, and signed away every claim to the fortune in front of three witnesses.
The estate she released did not vanish; under the will's terms it passed on to a conservation trust her grandfather had named.
Asked why she bothered with such formality, she said a decision this large should be made in the open, in writing, and once.
